theme: The kingdom divides; Jeroboam’s golden calves
readingInstruction: Read 1 Kings 12:1-14:20. The kingdom splits in two, and Jeroboam makes a fateful religious decision. Read the account of Rehoboam’s choice and Jeroboam’s golden calves carefully, because this sin will be named again and again through the rest of Kings.
settingTheScene: Solomon is dead, and his son Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be confirmed as king. The northern tribes ask for relief from the heavy labor and taxes Solomon imposed. What Rehoboam decides will tear the kingdom apart, as God had said through the prophet Ahijah. Around 930 BC, the nation splits into the northern kingdom of Israel under Jeroboam and the southern kingdom of Judah under Rehoboam. This begins the story of the divided kingdom.
observation: The people say, “Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father” (12:4).
Rehoboam rejects the counsel of the old men who served Solomon and follows the young men (12:6-14).
“My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions” (12:14).
“What portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel!” (12:16).
“So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day” (12:19).
Jeroboam says in his heart, “If this people go up to offer sacrifices in the temple of the LORD at Jerusalem, then the heart of this people will turn again to their lord” (12:26-27).
He makes two golden calves and says, “Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (12:28).
interpretation:
The narrator is clear that the split was God’s doing: “It was a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD.” It was judgment on Solomon’s idolatry. But that does not excuse Rehoboam. He had the chance to serve. The old men told him, “If you will be a servant to this people today and serve them… they will be your servants forever.” It was wise advice, and it is the way of a true king. But Rehoboam chose arrogance over service, the way of Pharaoh rather than of a shepherd. A proud word split a nation.

Jeroboam received a promise. Through Ahijah, God had said that if he walked in God’s ways, he would have “an enduring house, as I built for David.” It was a remarkable offer. But Jeroboam did not trust it. He feared that if the people went to Jerusalem to worship, they would go back to Rehoboam. So he set up his own religion for political reasons: two golden calves at Bethel and Dan, his own priests, and his own festival. “He had devised from his own heart.” It was convenient, efficient, and idolatrous.

This is the “sin of Jeroboam,” and it becomes the measuring stick for every northern king after him. Notice what he did. He took the story of the exodus, “who brought you up out of the land of Egypt,” and attached it to a calf. He did not reject the LORD. He reshaped worship to suit his needs. It is a warning about religion that is designed for convenience or politics. When we decide how God should be worshiped, we are no longer following him.

Chapter 13 shows the seriousness. A man of God from Judah prophesies against the altar, but he is deceived by an old prophet and killed by a lion. The message is that obedience to God’s word must be complete. And chapter 14 ends with the death of Jeroboam’s son and the prophecy that God will “give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, which he sinned and made Israel to sin.”
connection: Jesus is the king who came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45), where Rehoboam threatened scorpions. He is the true shepherd, who united what was divided: “He himself is our peace, who has made us both one” (Ephesians 2:14). Jesus said that true worshipers “will worship the Father in spirit and in truth” (John 4:23-24), not in a religion of our own devising. Paul warns of a religion of “self-made” worship (Colossians 2:23).
application:
Ask where you are tempted to answer pressure with pride instead of service.

Consider whether you have shaped your faith around convenience rather than God’s word.

Pray for the unity of Christ’s church, divided in many ways.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from Rehoboam’s pride and Jeroboam’s convenient religion.
Ask him to teach you to serve and not to rule harshly.
Ask him to help you worship him as he has revealed.
